question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
One group of the club has raised an undigestible criticism against the manager.
option_1: An undigestible criticism would have been raised by one group of the club against the manager.
option_2: An undigestible criticism was being raised by one group of the club against the manager.
option_3: An undigestible criticism had been raised by one group of the club against the manager.
option_4: An undigestible criticism has been raised by one group of the club against the manager.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. An undigestible criticism has been raised by one group of the club against the manager.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "One group of the club has raised an undigestible criticism against the manager" is in the Present Perfect Tense (Subject + has/have + V3 + Object).

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + has/have + V3 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "an undigestible criticism" becomes the subject; since it is singular/uncountable, the auxiliary is "has been"; the verb "raised" is already the past participle (V3); and "one group of the club" becomes the agent introduced by "by".
◦ Passive: An undigestible criticism has been raised by one group of the club against the manager.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "would have been raised" is the passive form used for the Conditional Perfect / third conditional, not the Present Perfect Tense of the original sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "was being raised" is the passive of the Past Continuous Tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "had been raised" is the passive of the Past Perfect Tense, which requires a past time reference, not present relevance as in the original sentence.

NOTE

• In Present Perfect passive constructions, the auxiliary "has" is used with singular/uncountable subjects and "have" with plural subjects.

• Words like "already", "just", "yet", "since", "for" commonly signal the Present Perfect Tense and should alert you to use has/have + been + V3 in the passive.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Vinay missed his flight but good luck came to him from bad circumstances as the flight crashed in the sea.
option_3: it was a blessing and a curse
option_4: it was a blessing in disguise
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. it was a blessing in disguise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a blessing in disguise" means something that seems bad or unlucky at first but turns out to be good or beneficial in the end. (मुसीबत में भी छिपा फायदा)
◦ Example: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise — he started his own business and became far more successful.

• In the given sentence, Vinay missing his flight seemed unfortunate, but it turned out to be lucky because the flight later crashed in the sea — this is exactly the sense of "a blessing in disguise", matching the underlined segment "good luck came to him from bad circumstances".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "A tinker's curse" (बेकार की चीज़): something worthless or of no value at all — unrelated to the sense of hidden luck.

• Option 2: "Counting one's blessings" (जो कुछ है उसके लिए आभारी होना): to be grateful for what one already has, rather than complaining — this does not capture the idea of a disguised stroke of luck.

• Option 3: "A blessing and a curse": used for something that has both good and bad effects at the same time, not something that appears bad but is actually good.

NOTE

• Other common idioms of luck/fortune asked in SSC: "a stroke of luck" (an unexpected fortunate event), "born with a silver spoon in one's mouth" (born into wealth), and "to strike gold" (to discover or achieve something very valuable or profitable).

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A.The Olympic Games have come to be regarded as the world's foremost sports competition.
B.Olympic Games is an athletic festival that originated in ancient Greece and was revived in the late 19th century.
C.Before the 1970s, the Games were officially limited to competitors with amateur status, but in the 1980s many events were opened to professional athletes.
D.Currently, the Games are open to all, even the top professional athletes in basketball and football (soccer).
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. BCDA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence B is the ideal opener, as it introduces the topic in general terms — "Olympic Games is an athletic festival that originated in ancient Greece..." — giving the reader the basic background before any specific detail is discussed.

• Sentence C logically follows B, since it develops the history further in chronological order — describing the shift "before the 1970s" from amateur-only status to the 1980s opening of events to professionals.

• Sentence D continues this timeline into the present with the word "Currently", describing today's fully open participation, including top professionals in basketball and football.

• Sentence A works best as the concluding, summarising statement — "The Olympic Games have come to be regarded as the world's foremost sports competition" — a broad concluding remark that fits only after the historical development has been laid out.

• Thus the coherent, logically flowing order is: B → C → D → A.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (ABDC) is incorrect because starting with the concluding statement A before the reader has any context makes the paragraph illogical.

• Option 3 (CADB) is incorrect because starting directly with the amateur/professional history (C) without first introducing what the Olympic Games even are (B) leaves the paragraph without a proper opening.

• Option 4 (BDCA) is incorrect because it places D (the present situation) before C (the earlier 1970s–1980s history), breaking the natural chronological sequence.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always look for the sentence that introduces the subject in the most general terms — it is usually the opening sentence.

• Words like "Currently", "Therefore", "However", "Thus" are strong linking clues — they rarely start a paragraph and instead follow the sentence they logically connect to.

question: Identify the INCORRECTLY spelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Obssess.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Obsess" (O-B-S-E-S-S) — meaning to preoccupy or fill the mind of someone continually and intrusively.
◦ Example: She let the small mistake obsess her for the whole day.

• The given option "Obssess" wrongly doubles the "s" in the middle of the word (after "Ob"), which does not occur in the correct spelling. Spelling key: OB + SESS — only one "s" follows "Ob", and the doubled "ss" occurs only at the end.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Weave" is correctly spelt — meaning to form fabric by interlacing threads.

• Option 2: "Heave" is correctly spelt — meaning to lift or haul something heavy with great effort.

• Option 4: "Sieve" is correctly spelt — meaning a utensil with mesh or perforated holes used to separate solids from liquids or fine particles from coarse ones.

NOTE

• Other commonly misspelt words with double letters tested in SSC: "embarrass" (double r, double s), "harass" (single r, double s), "possession", "occurrence", and "necessary" (one c, two s).

• Always check for accidentally doubled or missing letters in the middle of a word — this is the most common trap in spelling-identification questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Earnestly
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Sincerely.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Earnestly" means in a sincere and intense manner; showing deep and serious conviction. (गंभीरता और ईमानदारी से)
◦ Example: He earnestly requested the committee to reconsider its decision.

• "Sincerely" carries the same sense of genuine, heartfelt seriousness, making it the closest synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Wordily" (शब्दाडंबर से): using more words than necessary; wordy — unrelated to sincerity.

• Option 2: "Ambiguously" (अस्पष्ट रूप से): in a way that is open to more than one interpretation — nearly opposite in sense, since earnestness implies clarity of intent.

• Option 3: "Verbosely" (वाचालता से): using or containing more words than needed; wordy — again refers to excess of words, not sincerity.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Earnestly" useful for SSC: "seriously", "fervently", "zealously", "wholeheartedly".

• Do not confuse "earnestly" (sincere/serious) with "earnings" or "earnest money" (a deposit) — these are unrelated word forms that sometimes cause confusion.

question: Identify the sentence with correct spellings.
option_1: There was not enouf food in the beggar's house.
option_2: There was not enough food in the beggar's house.
option_3: There was not enauf food in the beggar's house.
option_4: There was not enoufh food in the beggar's house.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. There was not enough food in the beggar's house.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Enough" (E-N-O-U-G-H) — meaning as much or as many as required; sufficient.
◦ Example: There is not enough time left to finish the project today.

• Spelling key: the word ends in the silent letter combination "-ough", pronounced as "uff", which is a common irregular English spelling pattern.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Enouf" is incorrect — the ending has been wrongly simplified to "-ouf" instead of the correct "-ough".

• Option 3: "Enauf" is incorrect — the vowel combination "au" wrongly replaces the correct "ou", and the ending drops the "gh".

• Option 4: "Enoufh" is incorrect — the letters of the ending "-ough" have been jumbled into "-oufh".

NOTE

• Other common "-ough" words tested in SSC with varying pronunciations: "though" (oh), "through" (oo), "rough" (uff), "cough" (off), "bought" (aw).

• These words are frequently used as spelling traps because their pronunciation does not match their spelling in an obvious way.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A person whose age is between 70 and 79 years old
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Septuagenarian.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Septuagenarian" is a person who is between 70 and 79 years old. (सत्तर से उन्नासी वर्ष की आयु का व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: Her grandfather, a septuagenarian, still goes for a morning walk every day.

• The prefix "septua-" comes from the Latin "septuaginta", meaning seventy.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Aged" (वृद्ध): simply means old in a general sense, without specifying any particular age range.

• Option 3: "Pensioner" (पेंशनभोगी): a person who receives a pension, usually after retirement — refers to employment status, not a specific age band.

• Option 4: "Oldie" (बूढ़ा व्यक्ति/पुरानी चीज़, informal): an informal term for an old person or old thing, with no precise age range.

NOTE

• Related age-based one-word substitutes frequently asked in SSC: "Octogenarian" (80–89 years), "Nonagenarian" (90–99 years), "Centenarian" (100 years or more), and "Sexagenarian" (60–69 years).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
I play / cricket in / my childhood / with my sister.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. I play.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence refers to an action completed "in my childhood", a definite point of time in the past, so the verb must be in the Simple Past Tense, not the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule: When a sentence contains a past time expression such as "in my childhood", "last year", "in 2010", the main verb must take the Simple Past Tense (V2) form.

• The segment "I play" wrongly uses the present tense verb "play"; it should be corrected to "I played".
◦ Corrected sentence: I played cricket in my childhood with my sister.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "my childhood" is grammatically correct as written; it correctly indicates the past time frame.

• Option 2: "with my sister" is a correct prepositional phrase and needs no change.

• Option 4: "cricket in" is grammatically fine — "cricket" is the correct object of the verb, and "in" correctly introduces the time phrase that follows.

NOTE

• Watch for time-indicating phrases like "in my childhood", "in those days", "years ago" — they are strong signals that the verb of the sentence must be in the Simple Past Tense.

• A very common SSC error-spotting trap is a present-tense verb used with a clearly past time reference, or vice versa.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Announced
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Declared.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Announced" means to make a public or formal statement about something; to declare openly. (घोषित करना/सार्वजनिक रूप से बताना)
◦ Example: The company announced its quarterly results this morning.

• "Declared" carries the same sense of making something publicly and formally known, making it the closest synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Estrange" (अलग करना/विमुख करना): to cause someone to become unfriendly or hostile, especially within a family — an unrelated meaning.

• Option 3: "Secret" (गुप्त): something kept hidden or not disclosed — nearly opposite in meaning to "announced".

• Option 4: "Hid" (छिपाना, past tense of hide): to conceal something from view or knowledge — again, opposite in meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Announced" useful for SSC: "proclaimed", "publicised", "broadcast", "disclosed".

• Do not confuse "announced" with its near-opposites "concealed" or "withheld", which are commonly placed as distractor options.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Crooked
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Twisted.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Crooked" means bent or twisted out of shape or out of place; not straight. (टेढ़ा-मेढ़ा/मुड़ा हुआ)
◦ Example: The old fence had become crooked after years of exposure to wind and rain.

• "Twisted" carries the same sense of being bent out of a straight or natural shape, making it the closest synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Admirable" (प्रशंसनीय): deserving of respect and approval — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 2: "Taken" (लिया हुआ): the past participle of "take"; unrelated in meaning to shape or straightness.

• Option 4: "Toasted" (सेंका हुआ): browned by exposure to heat, as in toasted bread — unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• "Crooked" also has a figurative sense meaning dishonest or not straightforward (e.g. a crooked politician) — SSC sometimes tests this secondary meaning too, with synonyms like "corrupt" or "dishonest".

• Other synonyms of the literal sense: "bent", "curved", "warped", "distorted".

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A.We recognise some aspects of an SF narrative with the realities of this world and some elements are estranged from the reality so as to take us to an unreal world.
B.Therefore, it is often suggested that 'cognitive estrangement' is a necessary means through which the SF is usually understood.
C.Science Fiction is a genre which manifests in itself the use of scientific premises often in a fantastical manner in a narrative.
D.It is highly seeped into the reality of this world.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. CDBA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence C is the natural opening line, as it introduces the topic itself — "Science Fiction is a genre which manifests..." — defining what Science Fiction (SF) is before anything else is said about it.

• Sentence D logically follows C, using the pronoun "It" to refer back to Science Fiction, adding that it is "highly seeped into the reality of this world".

• Sentence B follows next, beginning with the connector "Therefore", which draws a conclusion from the idea in D — that because SF is seeped into reality, "cognitive estrangement" is suggested as the means to understand it.

• Sentence A comes last, as it explains and elaborates on the concept of "cognitive estrangement" introduced in B, describing how we recognise real-world aspects alongside estranged, unreal elements in an SF narrative.

• Thus the coherent order is: C → D → B → A.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (BCAD) is incorrect because it opens with "Therefore", a concluding connector, which cannot logically begin a paragraph.

• Option 3 (DACB) is incorrect because it opens with the pronoun "It" in D without first establishing what "It" refers to.

• Option 4 (ADBC) is incorrect because it places the definition of Science Fiction (C) at the very end, after the concept has already been discussed, which is illogical.

NOTE

• In para-jumbles, a sentence beginning with a pronoun ("It", "This", "They") or a connector like "Therefore", "However" almost never opens the paragraph — look for its antecedent among the other sentences first.

• The sentence that defines or introduces the core subject in general terms is usually the correct opening sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The Princess firmly held the ______ in her hands.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. rein.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Rein" refers to the long, narrow strap attached to a horse's bridle, used by the rider to control and guide the horse. (लगाम)
◦ Example: The Princess firmly held the rein in her hands as she rode across the field.

• Since the sentence describes something physically "held ... in her hands", and it fits the context of controlling something (as one holds a horse's rein), "rein" is the only word that makes sense here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Rain" (बारिश): water falling from the sky as precipitation — cannot be "held in one's hands".

• Option 2: "Ran" (दौड़ा, past tense of run): a verb, not a noun, and grammatically cannot fill a blank after "the" and before "in her hands".

• Option 3: "Reign" (शासनकाल/शासन करना): the period during which a monarch rules, or to rule as a monarch — an abstract concept that cannot be physically held.

NOTE

• "Rain", "reign" and "rein" are classic homophones (same pronunciation, different spelling and meaning) frequently tested in SSC fill-in-the-blank questions.

• Memory aid: "rein" (with an "i") relates to riding and control; "reign" (with a "g") relates to a ruler's rule; "rain" is the weather phenomenon.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The historians / are a great / asset to the/ field of academia.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The historians.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence makes a general statement about historians as a class/profession as a whole, not about any specific, previously mentioned group of historians.

• Rule: The definite article "the" is not used before a plural countable noun when speaking generally about all members of that class. The article is dropped, and the plural noun is used alone.
◦ Example: Teachers play a vital role in society. (NOT: The teachers play a vital role in society — unless referring to specific, already-identified teachers.)

• Applying the rule here: since the sentence refers to historians in general, the correct segment should simply be "Historians", without "The".
◦ Corrected sentence: Historians are a great asset to the field of academia.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "field of academia" is grammatically correct; "the" is rightly used here because it refers to the one specific, definite field being discussed.

• Option 2: "are a great" is grammatically correct; the plural verb "are" correctly agrees with the plural subject.

• Option 3: "asset to the" is grammatically correct as part of the phrase "a great asset to the field".

NOTE

• The definite article "the" IS used before a plural noun only when a specific, identifiable group is meant, e.g. "The historians who attended the conference presented new findings" (a specific group).

• This general-vs-specific use of "the" before plural/uncountable nouns is one of the most frequently tested article rules in SSC error-spotting questions.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A formal agreement between two or more nations or peoples
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Pact.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Pact" is a formal agreement, especially between two or more nations or parties. (संधि/समझौता)
◦ Example: The two countries signed a non-aggression pact after years of conflict.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Concord" (सामंजस्य/मेल): a state of peaceful agreement or harmony between people or groups — refers to a state of harmony, not a formal signed agreement itself.

• Option 3: "Bond" (बंधन): a shared feeling or connection, or a binding agreement/certificate of debt — too general and not specific to formal agreements between nations.

• Option 4: "Charter" (अधिकार-पत्र): a written document issued by an authority granting rights, or the founding document of an organisation — not specifically an agreement between nations.

NOTE

• Other related one-word substitutes frequently asked in SSC: "Treaty" (a formally concluded agreement between states), "Alliance" (a union formed for mutual benefit), "Armistice" (an agreement to stop fighting temporarily).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
The newspaper was read by me.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. I read the newspaper.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given passive sentence "The newspaper was read by me" is in the Simple Past Tense (Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject).

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "me" becomes the subject "I"; the past participle "read" is converted to the simple past form "read" (a word that is spelt the same in base, past, and past participle but pronounced differently as V2); and "the newspaper" becomes the object.
◦ Active: I read the newspaper.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "was reading" is the active form of the Past Continuous Tense, not the Simple Past.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "had read" is the active form of the Past Perfect Tense, which requires an earlier past action relative to another past action.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "will read" is the active form of the Simple Future Tense, which changes the time of the action entirely.

NOTE

• The verb "read" is unique in English — its base form, past form, and past participle are all spelt identically ("read"), but the past forms are pronounced like "red". Do not mistake this for an unchanged verb.

• Always identify the tense of the passive sentence first, then apply the matching active-voice formula for that same tense.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
In order to support countries with a concerted approach for an inclusive, and government-led assessment of post-disaster damages, losses, and recovery needs, as well as the development of a comprehensive recovery plan, the European Commission, the World Bank, and the United Nations adopted the Post Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA) process in 2008.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. complete.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "comprehensive" means including or dealing with all or nearly all elements or aspects of something; complete and thorough. (व्यापक/संपूर्ण)
◦ Example: The doctor recommended a comprehensive health check-up covering every major organ.

• In the passage, a "comprehensive recovery plan" refers to a fully complete, all-encompassing plan covering every aspect of post-disaster recovery — matching the synonym "complete".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "sustainable" (टिकाऊ): capable of being maintained over the long term without depleting resources — a different quality from completeness.

• Option 2: "clear" (स्पष्ट): easy to understand or perceive — refers to clarity, not scope or thoroughness.

• Option 4: "restricted" (सीमित): limited in extent or scope — this is nearly the opposite of "comprehensive", which implies wide, unrestricted coverage.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "comprehensive" useful for SSC: "thorough", "extensive", "all-inclusive", "exhaustive".

• Its antonyms include "partial", "limited", "incomplete" — these are commonly placed as distractor options in synonym questions on this word.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Mosquitoes __________ if there is no water logging.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. will not breed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence is a Conditional Sentence, Type 1 (real/possible future condition), expressing a general logical consequence.

• Rule — Conditional Sentence Type 1:
◦ If + Subject + Simple Present, Subject + will/will not + base verb

• Here the "if" clause "if there is no water logging" is in the Simple Present Tense, so the main clause must use "will/will not + base verb". Since the absence of water logging logically prevents mosquito breeding, the negative form "will not breed" correctly completes the sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "breed" is incorrect — a bare present-tense verb cannot correctly form the main clause of a Type 1 conditional, which requires "will/will not".

• Option 2: "will breed" is grammatically the correct structure but logically wrong — the absence of water logging should prevent, not cause, breeding, so this reverses the intended meaning.

• Option 4: "will have been breeding" is incorrect — this is the Future Perfect Continuous, an unnecessarily complex and contextually inappropriate structure for a simple general condition.

NOTE

• In Conditional Type 1, only "will/shall + base verb" (or its negative) is used in the main clause — never a continuous or perfect future form, unless a specific ongoing/completed nuance is intended.

• Mosquitoes breed in stagnant water, so logically the sentence should express prevention of breeding when there is no water logging — always check that grammar and logical meaning both agree.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution'.
Delegates of the conflicting countries formally meet at a conference to ironing out their differences.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. to iron out.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "to iron out" is an idiomatic phrasal verb meaning to resolve difficulties or differences through discussion. (मतभेद सुलझाना)

• Rule: When "to" is used as the sign of the infinitive (expressing purpose, as here — the delegates meet FOR THE PURPOSE OF resolving their differences), it must be followed by the base form of the verb, not the -ing (gerund) form.

• The underlined segment "to ironing out" wrongly combines the infinitive marker "to" with the gerund "ironing"; it must be corrected to the plain infinitive "to iron out".
◦ Corrected sentence: Delegates... meet at a conference to iron out their differences.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No substitution" is incorrect because the original segment does contain a grammatical error, as explained above.

• Option 2: "to ironed" is incorrect because the infinitive marker "to" must be followed by the base form of the verb, not the past participle "ironed".

• Option 3: "for iron in" is incorrect because it distorts the idiomatic phrasal verb entirely and produces an ungrammatical, meaningless phrase.

NOTE

• The infinitive of purpose ("to" + base verb, meaning "in order to") is a frequently tested SSC grammar point — never followed by "-ing" or a past-tense/participle form.

• Other common idiomatic phrasal verbs of resolving problems: "to sort out", "to thrash out", "to hammer out" (all meaning to resolve an issue through detailed discussion).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word from the sentence.
Dangerous
The traffic police have released a safe advisory that driving without seat belts is risky, beneficial, and fearful for human life.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Risky.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Dangerous" means likely to cause harm, injury, or death; involving risk. (खतरनाक)
◦ Example: Driving without a seat belt is dangerous, as it increases the chance of serious injury in an accident.

• Among the words used in the sentence, "risky" carries the closest meaning to "dangerous", since something risky involves the possibility of harm or an unwanted outcome.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Beneficial" (लाभदायक): producing good results or advantages — nearly opposite in meaning to "dangerous".

• Option 3: "Safe" (सुरक्षित): protected from danger or risk — the direct opposite of "dangerous".

• Option 4: "Released" (जारी किया गया): made available or set free — refers to the act of publishing the advisory, unrelated in meaning to "dangerous".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Dangerous" useful for SSC: "perilous", "hazardous", "precarious", "unsafe".

• This question tests careful reading — the sentence itself is illogical/contradictory (calling something both "beneficial" and "fearful"), so focus strictly on picking the word that matches the given target word's meaning, not on the sentence making perfect real-world sense.

question:
Choose the most appropriate meaning of the underlined phrase.
Many analysts are tipping stable, blue-chip companies to weather the storm.
option_1: to deal with a simple situation without being harmed
option_2: to deal with a situation without thinking
option_3: to deal with a difficult situation without being harmed
option_4: to deal with a simple situation without harming anyone else
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. to deal with a difficult situation without being harmed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to weather the storm" means to survive a difficult period or crisis successfully, without suffering serious damage. (मुश्किल हालात का डटकर सामना करना)
◦ Example: The company managed to weather the storm of the recession and emerged stronger.

• In the sentence, analysts predict that stable, blue-chip companies will successfully survive a difficult economic situation — matching option 3.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "weather the storm" specifically implies a difficult or challenging situation (a "storm"), not a simple one.

• Option 2 is incorrect because the idiom does not relate to "thinking" or the lack of it; it is about enduring hardship successfully.

• Option 4 is incorrect for the same reason as option 1 — it wrongly describes a "simple situation" and adds an unrelated idea about "not harming anyone else", which is not part of the idiom's meaning.

NOTE

• Other idioms built on "storm" commonly tested in SSC: "a storm in a teacup" (a lot of fuss over a trivial matter), "to take by storm" (to become very popular very quickly), "the calm before the storm" (a peaceful period before trouble begins).

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Any (1)_________ that revolves around a planet is a satellite. Mother Earth has a natural satellite in the moon. The earth is circled by a lot of man-made or artificial satellites. In 1957, the Soviet Sputnik was the first to be (2)_________ into space. There are currently a number of artificial satellites launched into space by various nations.

These satellites make it possible for us to talk on the phone, watch television, predict the weather, map the various surfaces of the earth and learn more about the world in which we live.

How does a satellite get started? It is typically launched into space by means of a rocket. After ascending into the thinner air layers above the earth, the satellite is released from the rocket. For a successful satellite launch, a rocket's speed is carefully calculated and controlled. Every object in space is pushed toward the earth's centre by gravity. The inertia of motion will propel the object into space if it has its own velocity of motion. When the orbital velocity is exactly right, these two opposing forces are balanced, causing the satellite to (3)_________ toward the earth while still hovering over its surface.

A satellite is said to be in geo-stationary orbit when it completes one revolution around the earth in a 24-hour period; It doesn't change when compared to a point on the surface of the earth. These orbits are typically used by satellites for communication and weather. The camera on the weather satellites takes pictures and sends them back to Earth. These are helping aid in weather forecasting. Radio receivers and amplifiers on communication satellites can (4)_________ waves back at a frequency that is different from the one the satellite received. The beaming frequencies of satellites that are 'parked' too close to one another must not interfere with one another. Television signals can be transmitted from one location to other using broadcast satellites, and scientists can (5)_________ scientific data from numerous satellites.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. object.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"Any (1) _________ that revolves around a planet is a satellite."** The blank needs a general noun that can refer to anything that orbits a planet — including both natural bodies (like the moon) and artificial satellites.

• "Object" is the most general and appropriate term, correctly covering both natural and man-made items that revolve around a planet, matching the passage's own next line referring to the moon as a "natural satellite".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "piece" does not fit — a "piece" refers to a part or fragment of something, not a whole orbiting body.

• Option 2: "being" is incorrect — "being" refers to a living creature or entity, which does not fit satellites (natural or artificial).

• Option 3: "body" is a plausible-sounding option (as in "celestial body"), but the passage's usage and the rest of the sentence flow more naturally and precisely with the broader, simpler term "object", which is the option marked correct in the official key.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read the full sentence (and often the next sentence too) before choosing the blank-filling word, since later context frequently confirms or eliminates options — here the next line about the "natural satellite" (the moon) confirms a general term is needed.

• Be careful of options that seem contextually close (like "body") but are not the option supported by the passage's exact wording and the official answer key.
